Experiments with clustering NVIDIA DGX Spark systems.

You can cluster 8 NVIDIA DGX Spark nodes together and get 1 TB of unified memory for running large, state-of-the-art models such as GLM 5.2, which is often discussed in the same class as Opus.

That said, this is not the same thing as a DGX Workstation with 784 GB of native memory. The total memory pool is larger, but inter-node communication adds latency and reduces effective bandwidth. In practice, the cluster is still slower than a workstation designed to behave as a single machine.

Right now I am running 8 nodes through a CRS804 switch with vLLM. The setup is up and stable across 4-, 6-, and 8-node clusters, which is enough to start a more structured benchmarking phase and compare the different configurations properly.

The current work is focused on baselining GLM 5.2 across 4-node, 4+1, 6-node, 6+1, 8-node, and 4+4 cluster layouts. The goal is not just to find out how large a model can be loaded, but to understand how throughput, latency, stability, network overhead, and parallelization efficiency change as the topology changes.

The key point is that the headline memory number is only part of the story. 1 TB of aggregated unified memory is impressive, but what really matters is how much of that memory the model can use effectively, and how much synchronization across nodes costs in real workloads.

For research, prototyping, and distributed inference testing, this is a very useful platform. It should be evaluated for what it is: a compact, flexible cluster, not a cheaper substitute for a DGX Workstation.

A first-of-its-kind open-source video generation model for embodied scenarios, using a Mixture-of-Experts design. 

LingBot-Video from @robbyant_brain, a Diffusion Transformer video foundation model built for embodied AI.

- The flagship 30B model activates only 3B parameters per generation, at 1M-token sequences

- At the same total parameter scale it reaches ~3X the inference efficiency of a Dense architecture at 1M-token sequences (3.18× vs. Dense 30B)

- Aesthetic-only reward models are why video generators fake physics, and this paper basically says so. Physical plausibility is not treated as vibes here; it gets scored through causality, object permanence, non-penetration and material realism.

- The model was not trained only on regular internet videos. Its pretraining data also includes 70,000+ hours of embodied footage, covering robot manipulation, navigation, and first-person action videos, so the model sees examples where movement actually changes the world.

- On RBench, it reports a 0.620 average, ahead of every listed open and closed model, while still losing some columns to Wan 2.6.

RL can't teach an LLM to solve problems it never solves. Robot policies suffer from exactly the same limitation.

The fix turned out to be almost embarrassingly simple: train the policy with diffusion noise during pre-training.

That's it.

The policy covers a much wider action distribution, RL finally has somewhere to search, and we fine-tune VLAs on real robots in under an hour.
